lesson.title: Meet the microcontroller
lesson.subtitle: The tiny computer that reads, decides and acts

video.title: Meet the microcontroller
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Mr Joseph — your computer studies teacher (main character)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, talks to the student)

scenes.visual: Amina at the school gate at sunset; a solar street light with a small panel on top flicks on as the sky darkens.
scenes.animation: Sky darkens; the lamp switches on; push-in on a small box on the pole.
scenes.narration: The solar street light outside our school comes on by itself at dusk. Nobody presses a switch. So who decides? A tiny computer, smaller than your fingernail.

scenes.visual: Darsi title card with the IoT track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark pops in; title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: meet the microcontroller, and write your first program.

scenes.visual: A small black chip grows large and opens up: a processor, a strip of memory, and rows of metal pins along its sides.
scenes.animation: Chip zooms in; each part highlights as it is named.
scenes.narration: A microcontroller is a whole small computer on one chip: a processor, a little memory, and pins, metal legs that connect it to the world. It runs one program all day, on very little power.

scenes.visual: A remote, a washing machine, a prepaid meter by a door and a car, each with a small glowing chip inside; then three small boards side by side on a desk.
scenes.animation: Each object pops in and its chip glows; the boards slide in last.
scenes.narration: You'll find them everywhere: in TV remotes, washing machines, prepaid electricity meters and cars. Boards like the micro bit, Arduino and ESP32 put one where you can program it.

scenes.visual: A board in the middle: a button and a light sensor wired in on one side, an LED, a buzzer and a small motor on the other.
scenes.animation: Arrows flow in from the inputs and out to the outputs.
scenes.narration: Each pin is an input or an output. Inputs bring the world in: buttons and sensors. Outputs act: LEDs, buzzers and motors. The micro bit even has a light sensor and twenty-five LEDs built in.

scenes.visual: A light meter beside each board: the micro:bit's scale runs 0 to 255, the Arduino Uno's 0 to 1023 in finer steps; a torch sweeps over both and the numbers climb.
scenes.animation: Torch sweeps; numbers count up on both scales.
scenes.narration: A microcontroller can't see light: it reads the sensor as a number, made of bits. The micro bit uses one byte: zero for dark, up to two hundred and fifty-five for bright. An Arduino Uno uses ten bits, up to one thousand and twenty-three.

scenes.visual: Mr Joseph holding a micro:bit; a screen beside him shows the reading falling from 200 to 20. Two answer cards drop in.
scenes.animation: The number ticks down; cards drop in with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! A micro bit's light reading drops from two hundred to twenty. Did it get darker or brighter?

scenes.visual: A hand passes over the micro:bit and the reading drops; the chip shows only the number, with a question mark over what to do.
scenes.animation: Hand slides over; number drops; a small program card slides in.
scenes.narration: Darker. Maybe a cloud passed, or a hand covered the sensor. The microcontroller only knows the number went down. What it does next is up to your program.

scenes.visual: Four steps on a circle, read, decide, act and wait, with a dot running round and round.
scenes.animation: The dot circles faster and faster.
scenes.narration: Every program sets up once. Then it loops forever: read the sensor, decide, act, wait a moment, and go round again, many times a second.

scenes.visual: The program as four blocks snapping together; beside them a lamp that lights when a hand covers the sensor.
scenes.animation: Blocks snap in one by one; the lamp follows the hand.
scenes.narration: Here's a night light. Forever: read the light level. If it's below fifty, switch the LED on. Otherwise, switch it off. Then wait a moment, and repeat.

scenes.visual: A phone browser with coloured MakeCode blocks and a simulated board beside them; then a sheet of paper with a hand-drawn flowchart: a diamond and two boxes.
scenes.animation: Blocks drag into place; the paper slides in and the flowchart draws itself.
scenes.narration: Build it as blocks in MakeCode, free in a browser, and test it on the simulator, with no board at all. Or draw it on paper as a flowchart: a diamond for each question, a box for each action.

scenes.visual: Mr Okafor beside Tunde's laptop: the program has no forever block. Outside the window the sky turns from afternoon to night. Two answer cards bounce in.
scenes.animation: Sky darkens; cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. Tunde's night light has no forever loop: it reads the light once, at the start. He switches it on in the afternoon. What happens when night falls?

scenes.visual: Four cards line up: a chip, an arrow in, an arrow out, a loop.
scenes.narration: Nothing: without the loop, it read once and stopped. Remember: a microcontroller is a computer on a chip, inputs bring the world in, outputs act, and the program reads, decides and acts, again and again.

scenes.visual: A student's notebook with a flowchart, a phone showing MakeCode's simulator with a light slider, and a micro:bit under a cupped hand with its LEDs lit.
scenes.animation: The slider moves down; the simulated LEDs light; the real ones follow.
scenes.narration: Try it yourself: draw your night light as a flowchart. Then build it in MakeCode, and slide the simulator's light level up and down. Got a micro bit? Cover it with your hand and watch, then change fifty to suit your room.

checkpoints.prompt: A micro:bit's light reading drops from 200 to 20. Did it get darker or brighter?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — on the micro:bit, 0 is dark and 255 is bright, so a drop to 20 means much less light.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — the reading goes up with light: 0 is dark and 255 is bright. A drop from 200 to 20 means it got much darker.

checkpoints.prompt: A night light reads the light only once, when it's switched on in the afternoon. What happens at night?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — it read the light once, saw daylight, and never checked again. The forever loop keeps it reading.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — without the loop, it reads only once, in daylight. It never sees the night, so the LED stays off.
